mechanism: Every upstream is a hardcoded literal, so the probe replaces the pinned server's `node-fetch` module and the global `fetch` with a controlled peer; the Go side gets seams for the three pinned bases whose defaults are the literals, and replays the same peer through a real listener. Rejected fetches are produced through a real CLOSED PORT on the Go side and through a throwing stub rule on the pinned side.

conventions.hosts: there is NO <mock> marker in this fixture: unlike the routes whose upstream is a caller- or secret-supplied URL, every upstream here is a pinned literal (api/text/image.novelai.net), so the recorded URL is the value the route constructed and the Go seam is pointed at the peer by the test
conventions.binary: the SSE frames, the JSON envelopes and the status phrases are recorded as base64 + SHA-256 + byte length and compared as bytes; the base64 image projection is a STRING body and is compared as text as well
conventions.outbound: `outbound` holds the requests the peer ANSWERED, in order, and is exactly what a Go peer must record. `outboundAttempts` is attempts = answered + rejected, which is the assertion the image route's second request needs. `outboundRejectedAttempts` separates the two because the pinned stub records a request before it throws while a closed port records nothing
conventions.count: the image route's outbound count is an ASSERTION, not a convenience: every no-upscale branch must be 1 and every upscale branch 2
conventions.syntheticBytes: every zip and png is generated by this probe (stored zip, fixed 1980-01-01 timestamps, a valid 1x1 greyscale PNG with a marker tEXt chunk), so the fixture carries no live provider output and no host-dependent byte

fields.reason: every branch differs in status: 200/400/500, and the streamed 401 becomes a 400
the whole stable header set (content type, content length, ETag, the security headers and Vary), minus the transport headers listed in `excludedResponseHeaders`
THE FRAMING: the forwarded stream is chunked with no content-length and no content-type, res.send is length-delimited. This is what a buffered capture cannot fake
the SSE frames, the JSON envelopes, the status phrases, the base64 image projections and the fallback image, compared as bytes
the stream ends cleanly after the final frame rather than being cut off
method, absolute URL, declared header set and the exact body of every request the peer ANSWERED, in order
THE COUNT: the image route's second request is an assertion. A no-upscale branch that made two requests, or an upscale branch that made one, fails here

the number of requests that were attempted and REJECTED. The stub records an attempt before it throws, so this is separated from `outbound` rather than silently merged: a closed port records nothing for the same attempt on the Go side
the scenario inputs: what the controlled peer was told to answer, including the synthetic archive bytes
the non-stream control is labelled in the fixture, so a reader can tell which capture proves the streaming branch

normalizations: A generate-image request with no seed (or a negative one) is randomized by Math.floor(Math.random() * 9999999999); the recorded request body carries `"seed":"<seed>"` and TestNovelAIGenerateImage randomizes the same way before comparing. It is the ONLY nondeterministic value in the domain.
transfer-encoding is recorded in `framing` rather than in `headers`, because Go's net/http exposes response framing as a struct field and strips it from the header map.
notRecorded: `if (!req.body)` on both routes: unreachable. bodyParser.json and bodyParser.urlencoded (server-main.js:110-111) assign `request.body = {}` before the content-type check, so a request without a body or without a content type reaches the handler with a truthy object. There is nothing to record and GoTavern's parser does the same.

a missing or non-string `model`: `getBadWordsList(req.body.model)` runs OUTSIDE the route's try block, so `model.includes` throws and the pinned process dies on the unhandled rejection. Probing it would kill the oracle mid-run, so it is a named Go deviation (500) rather than a recorded branch.

cancellation: the pinned handler aborts the upstream fetch through `request.socket.on(close)`. The controlled peer cannot hold a response body open without a tools/lib change, so a mid-stream client abort has no oracle here.

the status-LINE phrase: forwardFetchResponse assigns the upstream `statusText`, so the 401->400 stream rewrite reads `400 Unauthorized` on the wire while Go's net/http derives the phrase from the code and cannot be overridden. The status CODE and body are compared; the phrase is not recorded rather than recorded and ignored.
